page.mentor_intro: Acute interstitial nephritis is the great mimic of AKI: an idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reaction arriving 7-10 days after exposure to the culprit — antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs the commonest — with a sterile pyuria, modest proteinuria, and often systemic allergic features. The diagnostic trap is that the classic triad (fever, rash, eosinophilia) is frequently absent; eosinophiluria has fallen from favour, and biopsy remains the reference standard when suspicion is high and improvement does not follow drug withdrawal. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis is its insidious counterpart: progressive fibrosis from persistent insults — including long-term PPI exposure, analgesics, or aristolochic acid — presenting with concentrating defects and slowly progressive CKD.

teaching_points.claim: Drug-induced AIN is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction appearing 7-10 days after culprit exposure; drugs account for the overwhelming majority of AIN cases, with antibiotics, PPIs, and NSAIDs the leading causes.

The classic allergic triad is frequently absent; diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion (AKI after a new drug, sterile pyuria, modest non-nephrotic proteinuria), and biopsy is the reference standard when suspicion persists.

First-line treatment is withdrawal of the culprit drug with corticosteroids for persistent or biopsy-severe disease; early steroid responsiveness is the rule and delayed treatment risks incomplete recovery.

Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis — from prolonged PPI use, analgesics, toxins, or previous AIN — presents with tubular dysfunction (concentrating defects, acidosis, salt wasting) and progressive CKD requiring culprit withdrawal and supportive care.

uncertainties: Optimal steroid dose, duration, and whether early biopsy-guided therapy improves renal recovery lacks randomised evidence.
The causal contribution of PPIs to CKD progression at population level remains debated despite consistent observational signals.
mcq_angles: Culprit-drug timeline and the absent-triad trap.
Chronic TIN versus glomerular CKD patterns.
case_hooks: A patient on a new antibiotic develops AKI with sterile pyuria but no rash or fever; assess for AIN and plan management.
A long-term PPI user has slowly rising creatinine and bland sediment; evaluate chronic TIN and counsel on deprescribing.
page.gaps: The retained evidence is mechanism-focused; verify steroid protocols and biopsy thresholds against nephrology guidelines before approval.

page.mentor_intro: The small bowel is the longest segment of the gut and the rarest site for cancer — but primary gastrointestinal lymphoma is the exception, the GI tract being the commonest extranodal site of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The subtypes each carry a signature: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma as the dominant aggressive form; MALT lymphoma linked to Helicobacter in the stomach; enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (now MEITL) as the feared complication of coeliac disease; and Burkitt-type disease in the immunocompromised. Presentation is non-specific — pain, obstruction, bleeding, weight loss — so the diagnostic route runs through CT enterography, capsule endoscopy, and deep biopsy, with specialised cross-sectional imaging for staging.

teaching_points.claim: The GI tract is the most common extranodal site of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, though primary GI lymphoma remains a minority of all NHL; small-bowel primaries are disproportionately lymphomatous among small-bowel malignancies.
Principal subtypes: DLBCL (dominant aggressive form), MALT (gastric, H. pylori-associated), enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (coeliac-linked), and immunodeficiency-associated lymphomas.
Diagnosis requires endoscopic or surgical deep biopsy with immunophenotyping; cross-sectional imaging (CT/PET) and bone-marrow assessment stage the disease.

Treatment is subtype- and stage-directed: H. pylori eradication for early gastric MALT, chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP-type) for DLBCL, and surgery reserved for complications (perforation, obstruction, bleeding) rather than routine therapy.

uncertainties: Optimal management of refractory/relapsed enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is unsatisfactory and individualised.
The role of surgery versus endoscopic management for small-bowel obstruction in lymphoma is case-based.
mcq_angles: GI lymphoma subtypes and their associations.
Diagnostic pathway: enterography, capsule, deep biopsy.
Subtype-directed therapy including H. pylori eradication for MALT.

page.mentor_intro: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction is dysmotility masquerading as obstruction: coordinated propulsive activity fails without a mechanical blockage, producing recurrent distension, pain, vomiting, and malnutrition. Diagnosis is one of exclusion — imaging to rule out obstruction, then manometry, scintigraphy, and full-thickness biopsy when available to characterise the neuromuscular pathology. Secondary causes (scleroderma, amyloid, opioids, paraneoplastic) must be hunted. Management combines nutritional support, prokinetic trials, and small-bowel transplantation for intestinal failure; pyridostigmine's systematic-review evidence makes it a first-line pharmacological option.

teaching_points.claim: CIPO is a severe gastrointestinal dysmotility mimicking mechanical obstruction; diagnosis requires exclusion of mechanical causes followed by physiological testing (manometry, transit studies) and consideration of full-thickness biopsy.

Aetiology is primary (visceral myopathy or neuropathy) or secondary — scleroderma, amyloidosis, endocrine disease, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), paraneoplastic syndromes; identifying secondary causes redirects therapy.

Management is multimodal: dietary modification and enteral/parenteral nutrition, prokinetic agents (pyridostigmine supported by systematic review), treatment of secondary causes, and decompressive or transplant surgery for intestinal failure.
Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor enhancing cholinergic drive, has systematic-review support as a treatment option for CIPO directed at improving colonic and gut motility.

uncertainties: The evidence base for most prokinetics and novel agents (prucalopride, mosapride) in CIPO is small and heterogeneous.
Optimal timing and candidacy for intestinal transplantation in CIPO-related intestinal failure is individualised.
case_hooks: A patient has recurrent distension and vomiting with repeatedly 'normal' CTs; structure the CIPO work-up.
A scleroderma patient develops CIPO; identify the secondary mechanism and adjust management.
page.gaps: The retained abstracts do not include manometry-interpretation or transplant-candidacy criteria; verify against neurogastroenterology guidance before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Intestinal tuberculosis returns wherever tuberculosis returns: the ileocaecal region is its favoured site, and the challenge is twofold — diagnosing a disease whose presentation (chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, ileocaecal ulceration, strictures) is near-identical to Crohn's disease, and treating it with a regimen proven for pulmonary TB but applied to sites where drug penetration and duration questions persist. The diagnostic modernisation is molecular and endoscopic: tissue PCR, biopsy culture, and endoscopic-ultrasound guided sampling raise the yield over old serology. Mistaking Crohn's for TB commits patients to unnecessary immunosuppression; mistaking TB for Crohn's delays effective therapy — the differentiating review is the clinical lifeline.

teaching_points.claim: The ileocaecal region is the commonest site of intestinal TB; abdominal involvement accounts for about 11% of extra-pulmonary disease, with peritoneal and gastrointestinal forms predominating.

Diagnosis combines clinical-radiological suspicion with tissue confirmation: endoscopic biopsy for caseating granulomas, culture, and molecular (PCR) testing; peritoneal fluid analysis and ultrasound/CT-guided sampling assist in peritoneal disease.

The Crohn's-disease mimic is the central diagnostic trap; features favouring TB include pulmonary involvement, night sweats, ascites, patulous ileocaecal valve, and transverse ulcers, while longitudinal ulcers and perianal disease favour Crohn's.
Treatment follows standard anti-tubercular therapy (rifampicin-based multi-drug regimens); surgery is reserved for complications — obstruction, perforation, fistula, or bleeding.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of therapy for intestinal versus pulmonary TB, and the role of therapeutic trials, varies by guideline.
Diagnostic-test accuracy of individual modalities (PCR versus culture versus histology) varies with prevalence and technique.

An intestinal-TB patient develops persistent obstruction on therapy; outline the surgical-decision framework.

page.mentor_intro: Intra-abdominal infection is a two-front war: source control and antimicrobials, with source control the non-negotiable first front — no antibiotic regimen rescues an uncontrolled leak. The principles are physical: drain the pus, control the leak, restore anatomy, often staged with damage-control surgery in the unstable. Antimicrobial therapy covers the polymicrobial flora of secondary peritonitis (enteric gram-negatives, anaerobes, enterococci) with a source-appropriate, narrowable regimen; observational ICU cohorts show outcomes are dominated by severity, source control adequacy, and resistance patterns rather than agent choice alone.

teaching_points.claim: Source control — drainage of infected collections, definitive control of contamination, and restoration of anatomy — is the foundation of intra-abdominal infection management; antibiotics cannot compensate for inadequate source control.

Secondary peritonitis is polymicrobial; empirical regimens must cover enteric gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, with anti-enterococcal cover for healthcare-associated and high-risk cases, then de-escalate on culture.
Large ICU cohorts show mortality is driven by severity at onset, anatomical disruption extent, and inadequate source control — reinforcing early intervention and reassessment.
Duration of therapy shortens dramatically with adequate source control: 4-7 days is supported for most controlled intra-abdominal infections, extending only for persistent foci or inadequate control.

uncertainties: Optimal duration (short versus standard) in specific sources (pancreatic, biliary) continues to evolve.
The role of routine enterococcal and antifungal cover in community-acquired peritonitis is debated.
mcq_angles: What drives mortality in IAI cohorts.
Short-course therapy after adequate source control.

page.mentor_intro: Two devices carry most of the short-term mechanical-circulatory-support load. The intra-aortic balloon pump is the elder: counterpulsation inflating in diastole augments coronary perfusion and deflating in systole offloads the ventricle — modest support, easy to insert, but with the weakest outcome evidence (IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in post-MI shock). The Impella transvalvular axial-flow pump provides far greater flows and true ventricular unloading, at the cost of vascular complications, haemolysis, and bleeding. Combined IABP-plus-Impella strategies appear in systematic review as an escalation option; complications surveillance — access-site, haemolysis, limb ischaemia — is the defining ICU management skill.

teaching_points.claim: IABP counterpulsation augments diastolic coronary perfusion and reduces afterload; it provides modest haemodynamic support but IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in post-MI cardiogenic shock.

Impella axial-flow pumps deliver higher flows with active ventricular unloading across the aortic valve; they suit higher-severity shock but carry vascular-access, bleeding, and haemolysis complications.
Combined IABP-plus-Impella support is described in systematic review as an escalation strategy for refractory cardiogenic shock, adding pulsatility and afterload reduction to axial-flow output.

ICU management centres on complications surveillance: access-site bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis (plasma-free haemoglobin monitoring), device position (echo surveillance), and anticoagulation titration.

uncertainties: Whether Impella-based strategies improve mortality in cardiogenic shock (versus IABP or medical therapy alone) awaits definitive trials.
Optimal anticoagulation intensity and device-weaning protocols are centre-specific.

page.mentor_intro: Intra-articular injections for osteoarthritis sit on contested evidence: guideline recommendations diverge by region and economics, and the placebo-controlled literature is humbling — intra-articular saline performs comparably to corticosteroid, PRP, and hyaluronic acid in hip-OA network meta-analysis, reminding clinicians that much of the injection benefit is contextual. The defensible reading: corticosteroids give short-term symptom relief with diminishing returns and possible cartilage concerns with repeated use; hyaluronic acid offers a modest, delayed benefit some guidelines endorse and others reject; PRP shows promise in comparative meta-analysis but standardisation and cost limit routine use.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical-practice-guideline systematic review shows divergent regional recommendations for IA corticosteroid, hyaluronic acid, and PRP in knee OA — reflecting evidence uncertainty and economic context rather than clear efficacy differences.

Placebo-controlled network meta-analysis in hip OA found intra-articular saline as effective as corticosteroid, PRP, and hyaluronic acid — a powerful demonstration of contextual and placebo effects in injection trials.

In knee-OA comparative meta-analysis, PRP, bone-marrow aspirate concentrate, and hyaluronic acid outperformed corticosteroids for symptom outcomes, though heterogeneity and commercial bias temper the conclusions.

AAOS guidance supports corticosteroid use for short-term knee-OA symptom relief while not recommending routine hyaluronic-acid injection; repeated steroid injections carry diminishing returns and theoretical cartilage-harm concerns.

uncertainties: Whether PRP's comparative benefit survives rigorous placebo-controlled standardised-protocol trials is unresolved.
Long-term safety of repeated corticosteroid injections on cartilage remains incompletely defined.

page.mentor_intro: Two interventions dominate the first hours of intracerebral haemorrhage, and both are about stopping the bleed. Blood-pressure lowering — the INTERACT2/ATACH lineage refined to a target around 130-140 mmHg systolic, achieved smoothly and early — reduces haematoma expansion, the strongest modifiable predictor of outcome. Anticoagulant reversal is the second: warfarin reversed with PCC plus vitamin K, the DOACs with specific reversal agents (idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors), alongside platelet-transfusion caution — the PATCH lesson that indiscriminate platelet transfusion in antiplatelet-associated ICH may worsen outcome.

teaching_points.claim: Early, smooth systolic blood-pressure lowering to approximately 130-140 mmHg limits haematoma expansion, the strongest modifiable predictor of poor functional outcome.
Haematoma expansion is common within the first hours; blood-pressure variability and peaks are as important as the absolute achieved level — smooth control matters.

Anticoagulant reversal is urgent: vitamin K plus four-factor PCC for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors — with the agent's last-dose timing guiding urgency.
Platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH is not routine: the PATCH trial signal of harm without surgical indication cautions against indiscriminate transfusion.

uncertainties: How low to target systolic BP (intensive <130 versus 140-150) and the role of ultra-early aggressive lowering are refined but unsettled.
The ideal reversal strategy for factor-Xa inhibitor ICH when andexanet is unavailable follows PCC-based protocols.
mcq_angles: BP targets and the expansion-prevention rationale.
Avoiding BP variability in the acute phase.

page.mentor_intro: Acute ICH management beyond BP and reversal is a choreography of neuroprotection, surveillance, and escalation. The World Stroke Organization's synthesis of global guidelines provides the consensus frame: rapid CT, reversal of coagulopathy, BP control, and early neurosurgical assessment for cerebellar haemorrhage or deterioration — with inter-hospital transfer protocols for centres lacking neurosurgery. Raised intracranial pressure is managed with head positioning, osmotherapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol), and decompressive craniectomy for malignant MCA-pattern swelling; the cerebral-oedema guideline formalises selection and monitoring of these therapies. The through-line is organised systems — 'Code ICH' pathways compressing time-to-CT, time-to-reversal, and time-to-decision.

teaching_points.claim: Global stroke-guideline synthesis supports the core acute-ICH bundle: rapid neuroimaging, coagulopathy reversal, controlled BP lowering, structured observation, and early surgical assessment for cerebellar or deteriorating haemorrhage.

Intracranial-pressure management uses tiered escalation: head-of-bed elevation, sedation, osmotherapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol), CSF diversion where indicated, and decompressive craniectomy for refractory malignant swelling.
The cerebral-oedema guideline provides practical recommendations for selecting and monitoring osmotherapy and ICP-directed therapies in neurocritical care.
Cerebellar haemorrhage with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus is a surgical emergency for decompression and/or ventricular drainage — early recognition and transfer protocols determine outcome.

uncertainties: Whether ICP-monitoring-guided therapy improves functional outcome in ICH is unproven.
Optimal timing and selection for minimally-invasive haematoma evacuation remain under active trial evaluation.

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous-fluid prescribing is the commonest inpatient intervention and among the least audited: fluids are drugs with indications, contraindications, and toxicity — yet they are often prescribed 'to keep the vein open' by the most junior team member. The modern evidence frame is the four Ds and the harm narrative: the evidence base for exactly when and how much resuscitation fluid remains thin in multimorbid acute medicine, while harm accrues quietly through fluid accumulation — positive balance drives oedema, AKI, and delayed recovery even when each bolus looked reasonable. Perioperative and thoracic-surgery data anchor the optimisation principle: goal-directed, moderate-volume strategies beat both liberal flooding and dogmatic restriction.

teaching_points.claim: Fluid prescribing should follow drug-prescribing logic: assess need (hypovolaemia versus euvolaemia), choose fluid type deliberately (crystalloid default), define volume and endpoint, and review daily with a stop date.

The evidence base for exactly when and how much resuscitation fluid to give in acute medicine is limited; uncertainty should translate into small aliquots with reassessment rather than large empirical boluses.

Cumulative positive fluid balance is an independent harm driver: 'zero fluid accumulation' is the therapeutic goal in critical illness, with deresuscitation (fluid removal) a deliberate phase of care.
Perioperative evidence supports optimised, goal-directed moderate-fluid strategies over liberal administration; thoracic-surgery data show excess fluid drives respiratory complications.

uncertainties: Which dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, echo) best guide fluid responsiveness at the bedside remains practice-variable.
Optimal deresuscitation timing and triggers in established positive balance are not standardised.
